captions.text: Welcome to fraktul.
This is fraktul's own map, drawn by fraktul, so everything you see here is real.
Everything starts with one file.
You describe your system as blocks: each one has a title, a status, a short summary, and the files and functions it lives in.
The file sits in the same repository as the code, so it changes in the same pull requests.
Before anything is drawn, the check reads the model and tries every reference in it.
If a file was moved, or a function was renamed, the check fails and names the block to fix.
It also lists the files the model does not mention yet, so new code cannot hide.
Run it in CI, and the map can never quietly drift from the code.
The build reads the model, and then the code it points at.
It finds every function, what each file imports, and who calls whom.
From that it generates the levels under your blocks: a diagram of the files, then a diagram of the functions in each file, then the source itself.
None of it is written by hand, so none of it goes stale.
All of that lands in one page.
Someone new can start at the top and click their way down, one level at a time, from the big picture to a single line of code.
Hovering a block shows what is inside before you open it, and the Up button always takes you back.
A tour is a path through the map, like this one.
Each step can carry narration, and fraktul speaks it with a neural voice that runs on your own machine.
The highlight moves as the voice talks.
And when a person explains it better, anyone can record a walkthrough of their own, with their voice and every click saved together.
Finally, the map goes out the door.
Run it live while you edit, build a static folder for any host, or pack everything into a single HTML file you can send.
Where to next?
Pick a tour to go deeper.
Let's open the model file.
Every block in your system is a node.
Its id is short, lowercase, with underscores, because that same id is what you write in the diagrams.
Give it a title people understand, and a one or two sentence summary: that summary is what the side panel shows, and what search finds.
Each block says how real it is.
Built means it is running.
Prototype means it works but is not finished.
Planned and proposed are drawn dashed, so nobody mistakes a plan for a system.
External marks things you rely on but do not own.
The kind, a component, a data store, a person, a service, changes the shape it gets in the 3D view.
A block can carry a diagram, written in ordinary Mermaid, the diagram language many tools already read. fraktul adds no new syntax.
It just notices when a box has the same id as another block, and turns that box into a door you can open.
How diagrams chain together has its own tour.
Anchors are what keep the map honest.
A block lists the files and functions it lives in, the data it reads, the docs that explain it, and the decisions behind it.
Functions are written as a path, a hash, and the name.
A map can span several repositories: each one gets a key and a path, and anchors name the repo they live in.
The check tries every anchor on every run.
A number typed into a map is wrong the day it changes.
So fraktul reads facts while it builds.
Point adrs_dir at your decision records and they are listed, searchable, and linked from the blocks that name them.
For anything else, a small live module next to the model returns tables, lists and bars, read straight from the project.
Tours sit at the bottom of the same file.
Each step names the diagram to show, the boxes to light up, a title, and a line of text for the card.
Steps can branch into other paths, or into other tours.
Add a say line, and the step can be spoken.
Write what a guide would say out loud, which is more than the card shows.
fraktul reads each diagram the way Mermaid does, statement by statement.
It keeps track of every box, every edge, and a few special comments.
Because it only reads ids, you can write Mermaid the way you always have.
When a box has the same id as a block, it becomes a door.
It gets a small badge, hovering shows a preview of the diagram inside, and clicking opens it.
You can even leave the label out, and fraktul fills in the block's title for you.
That is the whole trick that lets you build high level diagrams out of smaller ones.
Sometimes an arrow should land on one particular piece inside a block.
Write the block id, a slash, and the inner box.
When that block is drawn open, the edge lands exactly there.
When it is closed, the edge lands on the block.
The check makes sure the inner box really exists.
Not every box is a block.
A comment that starts with at link ties a plain box to a file, a function, or a decision record.
Click it, and you go straight to that code.
This map is full of them: open the Build the map block, and each step links to the function that does it.
And at expand draws another block's whole diagram inside this one, as a group.
So a big overview can be made of the same small diagrams the teams keep up to date, with nothing copied and nothing to keep in sync.
Below your last block, the code takes over.
A block with files gets a generated diagram of those files.
Each file opens into its functions and who calls whom.
Each function shows its callers, the functions it calls, and its source, with every call a link.
You write the top, the code writes the bottom.
This is the page you are using right now.
The diagram in the middle is the level you are looking at.
Any box with the little badge opens into a level of its own: click it, and you go down.
Drag to pan around, scroll to zoom, and press zero to fit the diagram to the screen again.
Not sure if a block is the one you want?
Rest the mouse on it.
After a moment a preview appears with a small drawing of what is inside, and its summary.
Move away, and it goes.
However deep you go, you can always climb back.
The Up button at the top left takes you up one level.
The breadcrumbs next to it jump straight to any level above.
On the keyboard, Escape or Backspace do the same.
And the address bar follows you, so you can share a link to exactly where you are.
On the right, the details panel tells you about what you are looking at: its summary, its files and functions, its docs, and the decisions behind it.
Click a plain box to see its details instead.
When you want the whole screen for the diagram, hide the panel with the button at the top right, or press backslash.
Looking for something by name?
Press slash, and type.
Search covers every block, every file, every function, and every decision record, and takes you straight to it, opening every level on the way.
Press three, or the 3D button, and the same level becomes a small city you can fly through.
Blocks become buildings, data becomes stores, and the arrows become streams of light.
Drag to look around, use W A S D to move, and click a building to fly into it.
If you would rather look around without holding the button down, press L to lock the mouse, and Escape to let it go.
The Tours button lists guided paths like this one.
Read them at your own pace, or press Listen to hear them, with captions, and the camera following along in 3D.
The tour card can be dragged by its title bar, and folded down when it is in the way.
And the recorder lets you make tours of your own.
Narration starts as text on a tour step, in a field called say.
Write it the way you would explain it to a new colleague, standing at a whiteboard.
Inside the text, a pair of double square brackets with box ids moves the highlight at that exact moment of the speech.
Run fraktul voice, and the narration is split into sentences.
Each cue stays attached to the sentence it sits in.
Codes and numbers are read out digit by digit, and words the voice gets wrong can be spelled out the way they should sound.
Each sentence is spoken by Kokoro, a small neural voice model, running on your own Mac's GPU through M L X.
Nothing is sent anywhere.
You pick the voice in the model file; this one is called Emma.
Every spoken sentence is kept in a cache, keyed by its text and the voice.
Change one sentence in a long tour, and only that sentence is spoken again.
The rest comes straight from the cache, so re-running the voice after an edit takes seconds.
The sentences are joined into one short audio file per step.
Because each sentence was spoken on its own, fraktul knows exactly when each one starts and ends.
So the captions change on the right word, and the highlight moves the moment the voice names a block.
The check starts by loading the model.
Then it tries every anchor and every link: each file must still be in the repository, and each function must still be in its file.
Rename a function the map names, and the check fails, telling you exactly which block to fix.
Inside the diagrams, every at link must name a box that is really there, every block slash inner box must exist in that block's diagram, and every at expand must be a block with a diagram of its own.
Tours are checked too.
Each step's view must be a block with a diagram.
Every box it lights up, and every cue in its narration, must be in that diagram.
And every next step and branch must lead somewhere real.
Coverage works the other way round.
You tell fraktul which folders count, and it lists every file there that no block mentions yet.
Run the check with strict, and those fail too, so new code always lands on the map.
With expect, a team can set its own bar: how many levels deep each top block must go, and how many tours the map must have.
This map, for example, asks for eight tours.
All of this ends in one answer, pass or fail, with a list of what to fix.
Put it in your CI, next to the tests, and nobody can merge a change that breaks the map.
Some explanations are best in a person's own words.
Open Tours, and press Record a walkthrough. fraktul records your microphone, and every level you open, every block you hover, and every block you click, with the exact time.
When you stop, play it back, and save it.
Saving downloads one file.
One command imports it next to the model, and you commit it like any other change.
The next build lists it under the tours.
Play the recording, and the map follows your voice: the same levels open, the same blocks light up, at the same moments you clicked them.
It is the closest thing to sitting next to you.
Everything goes through one command line tool.
Run fraktul dev with your model, and the map opens in the browser.
Edit the model or the code, and the page rebuilds by itself.
Fraktul build writes a plain folder of files: the page, its diagrams, the narration audio, and the libraries it needs, with nothing loaded from anywhere else.
Put it on any static host.
This site is built and deployed that way by CI, with a preview for every pull request.
Sometimes you just want to send the map to someone.
Fraktul artifact packs the page, the data and the diagram library into a single HTML file that opens anywhere, with no server at all.
And when the code is private but the map should be shared, build in public mode.
The blocks, the diagrams and the tours stay; the source code and the links into the repository are left out.
